name: Signbook
powers: Formulas and signs for 'signing' wounds, bleeding, illness, and fire.
description: A signbook (signeringsbok), a hand-copied Swedish book of signs used by folk healers and 'kloka gummor', the wise women and men of the parish. The volumes collected prayers, magical signs, and formulae for 'signing' wounds, bleeding, disease, and fire. Several Swedish signbooks from the 17th to 19th centuries survive in archives, mixing Christian prayers with folk-magical practice. The practice of 'signing' — speaking or drawing a fixed formula over the ailing part — was the ordinary work of the kloka, who might be consulted when the parish priest could not help. Some books were copied from one another for centuries, and a famous line of them descends from the so-called Lappman Jon Johansson, whose signerier, printed in 1917, collected the oldest Swedish formulas. The books were practical manuals: they list what to speak for a bleeding wound, a burn, snakebite, and a house on fire, always in a mixture of biblical words and older charms.
source: Swedish folk-medicine collections (e.g. Nordiska museet, Riksarkivet)

name: Rune Calendar
powers: Read like a perpetual printed almanac of the church year.
description: A rune calendar (runkalender or runstav), a perpetual almanac carved on a long wooden or horn staff, used in Sweden from the Middle Ages into the nineteenth century. Each year's structure was fixed with runes: one rune row marked the weekdays, another the golden numbers that place the movable feasts. The staff was read like a printed calendar and was long carried by Swedish farmers and seafarers. The weekday row used one rune for each day of the week, while a second row of nineteen runes showed the golden numbers, so that Easter and the other moveable feasts could be found for any year. Because the calendar was carved once and worked forever, the runstav was cheap and durable, and it travelled from the farmhouse to the boat, where it helped sailors keep the church feasts at sea. Such calendars were still in use in the nineteenth century, and they are prized today as some of the last living carriers of the old rune row.
source: Museum collections of rune calendars (e.g. Nordiska museet)

name: Troll Porridge Bowl
powers: Appeases the tomte so the farm prospers.
description: At Christmas, Swedish farm families set out a bowl of rice porridge with butter for the tomte, the farm's household spirit. The bowl was left in the attic, the barn, or by the hearth; if the butter was hidden or the porridge forgotten, the tomte was said to abandon the farm or work mischief. The custom, documented across Sweden into the twentieth century, is the subject of many tomte tales. The offering was made on Christmas Eve or Christmas night, and the family looked the next morning to see whether the porridge had been eaten; the tomte, a small bearded figure who watched over the farm, was easy to offend and quick to reward a well-kept household. Tales tell of the tomte thrashing the hired girl who hid the butter, or blessing the family that always remembered his bowl, so that the porridge became the heart of the farm's winter ritual. The custom survives today in the small bowl of rice porridge still set out in many Swedish homes.
source: Swedish Christmas custom and tomte tales

name: The Magic Churn
powers: Dairy magic that brings or steals the butter.
description: A butter churn that witches were believed to bewitch or to work from afar. In Swedish folk belief a witch (trollkona) could send a 'mjölkhare', a butter or cream hare, to steal milk from neighbours' cows and churns, or charm a churn so that butter would not come. Counter-magic included heating a knife in the fire and running it through the churn to break the spell. The milk hare — a small creature conjured by magic — was sent to suck the neighbours' cows dry or to draw the cream from their churns into the witch's own. When a churn refused to give butter, the household suspected such theft, and the remedy was to strike the churn with a red-hot iron so that the witch felt the blow wherever she sat. The belief belongs to the wider Scandinavian complex of milk magic, in which the daily dairy work was watched as closely as any field, and a neighbour could be quietly accused of prospering at the cost of others.
source: Swedish folk belief about milk and butter magic

name: Witch Broom
material: Birch twigs bound to a handle
powers: Carries the rider to the witches' sabbath mountain Blåkulla.
description: The broom (kvast) that, in Swedish folk belief, carried witches to Blåkulla, the witches' sabbath mountain, especially on Maundy Thursday before Easter. The 'påskkärring', the Easter witch, was thought to ride a broom, or a cow, goat, or pitchfork, to Blåkulla. People blocked chimneys and hid brooms behind stoves to stop the flights, and the belief shaped Sweden's Easter-witch custom. The journey was said to take place on Maundy Thursday night, when the witches flew to the mountain, danced, and made their pact with the devil; families therefore stopped up their chimneys, barred their doors, and hid every broom, for a broom left within reach could carry off the household's own luck. Children were forbidden to go out, and the custom of dressing children as Easter witches — with broomsticks and painted cheeks — grew directly out of this old night of fear. The belief is recorded in the witchcraft trials of the seventeenth century, where the flight to Blåkulla was confessed again and again.
source: Swedish belief in the Easter witches of Blåkulla

name: Knotted Rope Charm
maker: Tied by a 'wise' seller or Sami sorcerer
powers: Untying a knot raises wind; the third knot calls a storm.
description: A rope or cord with three knots, tied by a 'wise' seller and sold to sailors as a wind charm. Untying the first knot raised a gentle wind, the second a stronger breeze, and the third a storm, so prudent captains kept the third knot tied. The three-knotted wind cord is documented in Nordic and Sami maritime folklore and was often credited to Lapp (Sami) sorcery. Olaus Magnus drew and described the custom in 1555: a seaman from the north sold a cord of three knots to sea captains, warning that the third must never be loosed unless the ship stood in danger. The poet Petter Dass and later collectors repeated the account, and the 'wind knot' appears in accounts of Finnish and Sami magic, where the seller was sometimes said to have learned the skill from the Sami themselves. Frazer gathered the custom as the classic example of sympathetic wind magic, in which loosening a knot looses the wind the knot had bound.
source: Nordic maritime folklore on wind magic

name: The Church Bell Against Storms
powers: Its ringing breaks up storms, drives away evil, and helps stop fires.
description: Swedish church bells were believed to protect the parish: they were rung to break up thunderclouds, drive away storms and pestilence, and even to help stop fires. The casting of a new bell was accompanied by rites, and the bells were thought to carry a blessing that evil powers could not withstand. Ringing against bad weather ('ringning mot oväder') is recorded in many Swedish parishes. The sound of the consecrated bell was held to drive off the trolls and evil spirits that raised the weather, and the clergy were asked to ring while a storm passed, sometimes with a formula of words recited as the bell swung. When a fire broke out, the same bell was rung to alarm the parish and, in folk belief, to check the flames themselves. The rite of casting — pouring the bronze with prayers and watching over the new bell — made each bell a sacred object, and church bells were consequently treated with the respect owed to relics.
source: Swedish parish tradition of bell ringing against the weather

name: The Magic Scythe
maker: Given as a wonder-gift in the tale
powers: Mows grain by itself, without a hand to swing it.
description: A scythe in Swedish folktales that cuts grain by itself, without a hand to swing it. In the tale of the magic scythe, the wonderful tool performs the harvest work of many men, sparing its owner the labour of mowing. The self-working scythe belongs to a family of Swedish wonder-tools in which ordinary farm implements act on their own. In the best-known telling the scythe is a loan from the hidden people: an elf of the huldufólk gives a poor farmer a blade that mows his grain by itself while he rests, on the single condition that it be returned to the elf's clearing each evening. When the farmer breaks his word and hides the scythe, it turns on him and mows down his fences and his house until he begs forgiveness, and the elf strips the magic away. The tale thus joins the wonder-tool motif to the strict bond between humans and the hidden people, who give generously and punish broken trust without mercy.
source: Swedish folktale 'The Magic Scythe'

name: Silver Buckles
description: Silver buckles and clasps worn with Swedish regional folk dress, on belts, shoes, and collars. Such silver, often inherited and re-used across generations, was engraved with initials and dates and served as both ornament and stored wealth. Wealthy folk wore heavy rectangular 'spännen'; poorer folk wore simpler clasps. The buckles are a documented part of the folk-costume tradition. The silver was a family's movable fortune: a bride might receive buckles, brooches, and chains that were passed down and re-fashioned by local silversmiths, with the owner's initials and the year engraved on the face. Great regional pieces, like the broad buckles of Dalarna or Skåne, marked a wearer's home district at markets and church, and the weight of silver on a person's belt was read as a sign of standing. When the folk costume fell out of daily use, the buckles were kept as heirlooms, and they are still worn today at festivals and on modern folk-dräkt celebrations.
source: Swedish folk-costume and silver traditions

name: Bridal Crown
powers: Marks the bride as a crowned bride, bringing honour to the wedding.
description: The bridal crown (brudkrona), a crown of gilt silver or brass that Swedish churches owned and lent to brides for the wedding ceremony. The custom, recorded from the Middle Ages, made the bride a 'crowned bride' and the crown a symbol of honour and virginity. Rules sometimes required a fee, and the crown was kept locked in the church between weddings. The crown became common in Sweden only after the Reformation, when it spread from the nobility and the towns to country parishes in the seventeenth century; it was usually owned by the parish itself, lent out for the wedding and locked away again afterwards. Made of gilt silver with red and green glass set in imitation of gems, it recalled the crown of the Virgin Mary, and a bride who had once worn it was said to keep that honour for life. The fee charged for the lending supported the church, and the rules could be strict: the crown was returned the same day, and its use bound the bride to a good name.
source: Swedish church custom of the bridal crown

name: Swedish Folk Costume
material: Wool and linen with silver and embroidery
description: The Swedish folk costume (folkdräkt), the regional dress of parish and province, worn for work and festivals and gradually codified from the 18th century. Each district had its own colours, cut, embroidery, and accessories such as the flounced apron and the bodice. The national costume, the Sverigedräkt, was created in 1903 by Märta Jörgensen and has since been widely adopted. In the countryside the dress told every beholder where a person came from: the cut of the skirt, the shape of the bodice, and the colour of the stockings changed from parish to parish, and the right to wear certain garments was guarded with pride. Wool and linen were woven and dyed at home, while the silver buckles and brooches that fastened the clothes were the work of the village smith. When the folk costume died out in the later nineteenth century it was preserved by the museums, and in the twentieth it was revived for national holidays — most famously the blue-and-yellow Sverigedräkt, which remains Sweden's most worn ceremonial dress.
source: Swedish folk-dress research (e.g. Nordiska museet)

name: The Ljungby Horn
maker: Said to have belonged to a troll
powers: Drinking horn of the troll folk, kept in the church at Ljungby.
description: The Ljungby horn, a great drinking horn with gilded silver mounts that is kept at Trolle-Ljungby Castle in Scania (Skåne), southern Sweden. Legend says the trolls who live beneath the great boulder Maglestenen once feasted on golden pillars at Christmas, and that a stable hand who rode out on their feast night came away with their horn and their pipe. As he rode, the drink he was offered burnt his horse's flank like acid, and the trolls pursued him to the castle gate; when he reached the plowed field and rode a cross shape over it, the trolls could not follow. They cursed the castle — the horse and the rider died, and the castle burned three times — and the horn and pipe were kept within the walls forever after. The objects survive to this day and are shown to visitors as proof of the trolls' feast, making the horn one of the best-known relics of Swedish legend.
source: Småland legend of the Ljungby horn and pipe

name: The Ljungby Pipe
maker: Said to have belonged to a troll
powers: Blowing it was said to set people dancing against their will.
description: The Ljungby pipe, a whistle of carved bone or ivory kept together with the Ljungby horn at Trolle-Ljungby Castle in Scania, southern Sweden. In the legend the trolls beneath the boulder Maglestenen offered the pipe, together with their drinking horn, to a stable hand who came to their Christmas feast; it was playable from both ends and formed one half of the trolls' treasure. When the servant fled with the horn and the pipe, the trolls' pursuit broke against the cross-shaped furrows of the plowed field, and their curse fell on the castle instead. The pipe was long counted among the wonders of Trolle-Ljungby, kept beside the horn in a glass case that no one dared to open, for the trolls had warned that if the objects were ever removed the owner would meet great misfortune. Together the horn and pipe preserve the memory of a troll feast at a real Swedish castle.
source: Småland legend of the Ljungby horn and pipe

name: The Magic Table
aliases: Table, the Ass and the Stick
maker: Given as a wonder-gift in the tales
powers: Sets itself with food and drink at a word.
description: A table that sets itself with food, a recurring wonder-object of Swedish folk tales. At a word the self-serving table covers itself with dishes and ale, so the hero never goes hungry; the motif usually appears in tales where a magic object is given as a reward and later stolen and replaced with a worthless copy. It belongs to the family of self-working marvels in Swedish wonder-tales. The tale is best known through the Grimm brothers' 'Tischlein deck dich', but Swedish versions circulated widely: a poor man serves a spirit or a mysterious helper, and in reward receives a little table that feeds him at a word. A dishonest innkeeper or a jealous brother steals the table and leaves a common one in its place, until the hero recovers the true treasure by showing its power. The self-setting table is one of a trio of wonder-gifts — the table, the money-dropping ass, and the stick that beats — and its promise of endless food made it a favourite of hungry listeners.
source: Swedish wonder-tale motif of the self-setting table

name: The Golden Keys
powers: Unlock doors and rewards for the hero who wins them.
description: Golden keys that appear in a Swedish folk tale, unlocking a reward or a forbidden treasure for the hero who obtains them. The keys belong to the tale's wonder-logic: ordinary locks fall open before them, and possession of the keys brings the hero to fortune. The motif is told as part of the tale 'The Golden Keys'. In the Swedish version the humble meadow-maid Lena meets three fairies who give her a golden key to a magical dream garden, on the strict condition that she tell no one of it; when the young king falls into danger, she must break her word to save him, and her selfless choice earns her the king's hand. The key thus works as the fairy gift of the tale: a secret treasure that tests the holder's worth more than it rewards the greedy. The fairies belong to the älvor, the beautiful but otherworldly spirits of Swedish forests and meadows, who grant gifts only to those who keep faith with them.
source: Swedish folktale 'The Golden Keys'

name: The Queen's Necklace
maker: Court jewel, object of the tale
description: A necklace in a Swedish folk tale, worn by a queen and central to the story's test or reward. In the tale 'The Queen's Necklace', the necklace passes through the hands of the characters and its loss, theft, or recovery drives the plot. The jewel is a typical treasure of wonder-tales, standing for wealth, rank, and the queen's honour. In the Swedish telling the cruel king Hendrik gives his bride Blanzeflor a necklace of one hundred perfect pearls with the warning that her life hangs on it; the queen, finding her only joy in charity, gives the pearls away one by one to feed the poor. When the king discovers the empty string he condemns her to death, but the birds she has fed come to her cell, rescue her, and destroy the tyrant. The necklace is therefore the instrument of both the queen's imprisonment and her redemption — a chain of rank that a generous heart transforms into a ladder of rescue.
source: Swedish folktale 'The Queen's Necklace'

name: The Skin Satchel
maker: Sewn for a magical purpose in the tale
powers: Holds an impossible store or releases the tale's marvels.
description: A satchel made of animal skin that carries magic in a Swedish folk tale. In the tale 'The Skin Satchel', the humble leather bag turns out to hold an impossible store, or to have been sewn for a magical purpose, and its opening releases the story's marvels. The satchel is one of many everyday objects in Swedish wonder-tales that conceal power. In the Swedish version the poor Niklas sees a troll take six grains from a leather satchel and grow an entire field of wheat in minutes; to win the satchel he must keep hold of it through the long night while the trolls shake the ground, send ghostly apparitions, and howl like wolves, without letting go or speaking a single word. When dawn breaks the trolls retreat and the satchel is his, and its endless grain saves the starving village. The tale joins the wonder-bag motif to the classic ordeal of the trolls' night, where courage and silence win the treasure.
source: Swedish folktale 'The Skin Satchel'

name: The Magician's Cape
maker: Worn by the magician of the tale
powers: Lets the wearer fly, turn invisible, or work spells.
description: A cape that gives its wearer magical power in a Swedish folk tale. In the tale 'The Magician's Cape', the cloak lets the hero fly, become invisible, or work spells, and is won, lost, and recovered through the story's tests. The cape is a classic object of wonder-tales: a garment of ordinary cut that carries extraordinary ability. In the Swedish telling the ancient magician of the mountain keeps a black flying cape sewn from the wings of a thousand bats and stitched with thread spun from midnight; with it he soars over the treeline and across seas, and no one can follow him. The captive girl Astrid watches his habits, steals the key from his belt, and takes the cape for herself, flying to the kingdom to bring soldiers against him. She keeps the cape and becomes the kingdom's messenger, flying from village to village — the stolen wonder-garment turned from the tyrant's weapon into the servant of the free.
source: Swedish folktale 'The Magician's Cape'

name: The Barrel Bung
powers: Conjures food, drink, or gold for its owner.
description: A barrel bung, the wooden stopper of a cask, that works magic in a Swedish folk tale. In the tale 'The Barrel Bung', the small wooden plug proves able to conjure food, drink, or gold for its owner. It is one of the many humble objects that Swedish wonder-tales turn into providers of plenty. In the Swedish telling, famine has dried the parish of Bolinge while the rich Lady Skinflint's cows never fail; the boy Jerker discovers why — she keeps an enchanted barrel that gushes milk whenever the bung is drawn. When she hides the bung, the barrel is only wood and iron, and the king's men find nothing; Jerker must watch and wait until the bung is carried back, then seize it in a single dash. The magic bung, once stolen, feeds the whole starving village through the winter, and the boy is rewarded with wool and silver for his courage. The tale makes the smallest of farm objects the key to plenty and to justice.
source: Swedish folktale 'The Barrel Bung'

name: Nyckelharpa
maker: Swedish instrument makers, especially in Uppland
description: The keyed fiddle (nyckelharpa), a bowed string instrument with keys that stop the strings, played in Swedish folk music since the 16th century and especially associated with Uppland. Its buzzing drone strings and chromatic key rows give it its characteristic sound. It was revived in the early 20th century and remains a national instrument, played at dance and fest. The instrument's keys press tangents against the strings to change their pitch, while one or more drone strings ring beneath the melody, giving the nyckelharpa its humming, hurdy-gurdy-like timbre. Surviving church paintings and written sources place it in Sweden by the sixteenth century, and by the eighteenth the great three-row instruments of Uppland were played at village dances and weddings. When the tradition waned, the revival of the 1920s, led by makers and players such as Eric Sahlström, rebuilt the instrument for a new audience; today the nyckelharpa is taught in Swedish folk-music schools and played around the world.
source: Swedish instrument history and folk-music research

name: Dala Horse
maker: Carvers of the Mora region, Dalarna
description: The Dala horse (Dalahäst), the carved wooden horse of Dalarna, painted in red, white, blue, and green with a floral saddle. The craft grew from toys carved during long winter evenings in the 17th century into a famous local industry around Mora, where the horses are still hand-carved and painted. The Dala horse has become the best-known symbol of Swedish craft. The carvers of the villages around Lake Siljan — above all Bergkarlås, Risa, Vattnäs, and Nusnäs — made the horses from pine left over from furniture and clock-making, and by the early seventeenth century the toys were already being sold, the oldest written mention dating to 1623. The figure is hollowed out of two carved halves and glued, then painted in the kurbits folk style with a saddle of flowers and leaves. What began as a child's toy became, in the twentieth century, a national emblem, and the Nusnäs workshops still ship the red horse to buyers the world over.
source: Dalarna woodcarving tradition (Mora)

name: Midsummer Maypole
maker: Raised by the village at Midsummer
powers: Centre of the Midsummer dance and fertility rites.
description: The midsummer pole (midsommarstång or majstång), a tall pole decorated with greenery, flowers, and rings, raised on Midsummer Eve and danced around in Swedish tradition. Songs, ring-dances, and games circle the pole, and the custom is recorded in Sweden from the 17th century. The pole is central to the Midsummer celebration and its bonfire-night rites. The pole is decked with leaves and flowers and hung with two crossed rings, and the village raises it in the open place of the farm or village before dancing the ring-dances that circle it. The custom was already described in the seventeenth century, when the pole was sometimes called a 'majstång' even in midsummer, and scholars have read it as a survival of the old fertility rites of the turning year. Around the pole the shortest night is kept with music, flowers, and the bonfires that guard the livestock, and the maypole remains the fixed centre of every Swedish Midsummer.
source: Swedish Midsummer tradition

name: Yule Goat
description: The Yule goat (julbock), a goat figure of straw bound with red ribbon, made in Sweden at Christmas. The straw goat descends from older beliefs around Thor's goats and the 'julbock' who once brought the Christmas gifts before the tree took the role. Today the most famous example is the giant Gävle goat, erected and burned each December. In older custom the julbock walked the house at Christmastime, demanding drink and carrying the Christmas presents, and a man dressed as the goat was one of the stock figures of the old rural Christmas. The straw goat, made of bound and tied straw with red ribbon at the horns, is the decorative descendant of that figure, and it is hung on the tree or set beneath it as a charm of the season. Since 1966 the town of Gävle has raised a huge straw goat in its square each December, and its repeated burning by pranksters has made the Gävle goat a world-famous piece of Christmas folklore.
source: Swedish Christmas tradition of the julbock

name: The Troll's Mitten
description: A mitten that a troll or giant is said to have dropped and left behind, so large that a human could use it for shelter or sleep inside the thumb. The motif of the lost glove or mitten of the troll folk appears in Swedish tales as proof of the hidden people's size, and finding it is both marvellous and dangerous. In one telling a traveller lost in the woods finds shelter from the storm inside a huge abandoned mitten, only to learn at dawn that he has slept in the dropped glove of a jätte, one of the ancient giants of Swedish folklore. The giants and the trolls of Swedish tradition are close kin — both dwell in the mountains and the deep forest, and both are of impossible size — and the same lost-mitten story is told of each. The mitten is thus a story-teller's proof of the scale of the other world: a single dropped garment that shows how small the human world is beside the hidden one.
source: Swedish troll-tale motif of the lost mitten

name: The Bewitched Knife
powers: Steel laid across the cradle keeps the changeling away; a knife breaks spells.
description: An iron knife that Swedish folk tradition used against harmful magic, one of the many protective uses of steel and iron in Nordic belief. A knife or other steel object laid across a newborn's cradle was believed to keep the bortbyting, the changeling, from swapping the child, and similar iron was set under the birthing bed and over the stable door to hold off trolls and the mare. A knife was also run through a bewitched churn, struck into the threshold, or thrown over the roof to break a spell that had soured the milk or the luck of a farm. The sign-carved knife served the healer in 'signing' rites, where a knowledgeable woman or man traced protective marks and spoke a formula over the sick. Iron's power to turn the hidden folk and their magic is one of the oldest and most widespread motifs of Scandinavian folk belief, surviving into the 20th century in rural custom.
source: Swedish folk belief in steel against harmful magic

name: The Offer Stone
powers: Cups held offerings for blessing and healing.
description: The offer stone (offersten), a boulder with cup-shaped hollows where offerings were made. Hundreds of such stones survive across Sweden, often beside churches, springs, or old cult sites, and in places they are the only trace of a vanished place of worship. Small gifts of coins, food, butter, or tar were placed in the cups, sometimes on fixed holy days, and the stones were consulted for healing of people and livestock; in later Christian times they were avoided, or 'baptised' with a name to break their power. In some districts the cup-marks were called älvkvarnar, 'elf mills', from the belief that elves ground grain in them at night. The cup-marked stones, skålgropsstenar, are counted among Sweden's oldest cult objects, with the oldest hollows ground into the rock in the Bronze Age.
source: Swedish antiquarian and ethnological records of offer stones

name: The Holy Spring
maker: Natural spring, named for a saint
powers: Healing water for the sick who visit on the appointed day.
description: The holy spring (heliga källan), a spring or well that Swedish folk tradition credited with healing. Such springs, often named for a saint, were visited for cures on particular days, usually the saint's feast or a church holiday, and the water was drunk, bathed in, or carried home in flasks for the sick and the cattle. Pilgrims left offerings of coins, linen, or small crosses, often hanging them on a nearby tree, and some springs were said to swell, run warm, or glow before a miracle. When a cure failed, the spring might be slandered as having lost its power. Many Swedish holy springs became local pilgrimage sites that the church later absorbed by blessing them anew, or closed altogether, yet the custom of visiting them survived into the 19th and even the 20th century in parts of the countryside.
source: Swedish holy-spring tradition and place-name studies

name: The Kettle of the Underjordiska
powers: Returned filled with gold, or borrowed at a price.
description: A pot or kettle that the underjordiska, the hidden people beneath the earth, were said to borrow from farm households. In Swedish legend a woman lends a kettle to the hidden folk, often for a christening or a feast in their underground halls, and finds it returned filled with gold, a silver gift, or the sweet smell of their food — or learns that borrowing from them carries its own price. The motif of the borrowed vessel, known across Scandinavia, plays on the housewife's neighbourly duty to the hidden people and her reward or punishment for how she meets it. If she gave generously and asked no questions she was blessed; if she grudged the loan or told the world about it, the kettle came back fouled or the farm's luck turned. The borrowed kettle is one of the commonest objects in the story-world of the underjordiska.
source: Swedish legends of the underjordiska

name: The Troll Shoes
maker: Worn by a troll in the tale
powers: Let the wearer stride over mountains or move faster than thought.
description: Shoes worn by a troll in a Swedish folk tale. In the tale 'The Troll Shoes', the troll's footwear, or the wearing of it, lets a human stride over mountains or move faster than thought, and the shoes are won or put on during the tale's test. The wonder-shoes belong to a wider family of magic footwear in Nordic tales, where boots or shoes carry the wearer across any distance, the same gift that appears in tales of seven-league boots elsewhere in Europe. Winning them usually demands courage or a clever bargain with the troll, and wearing them well shows the hero's worth. The troll's shoes are a typical wonder-object of Swedish troll tales, where the hidden folk's tools are both a danger and a prize for the human who can take them.
source: Swedish folktale 'The Troll Shoes'

name: The Golden Cradle
description: A cradle of gold in a Swedish folk tale, in which a special child is laid and around which the tale's wonder unfolds. In 'The Golden Cradle', the precious cradle marks the child's destiny and the family's fortune, and its making or finding drives the story. The cradle, the most intimate of household objects, is here lifted out of the everyday into the realm of the marvellous, a sign that the child in it is no ordinary child. Tales of golden cradles and foundling princes appear across Europe, and in the Swedish version the treasure is bound up with the home it blesses. The golden cradle is an emblem of the wonder-tale's promise of wealth and favour, and of the belief that the household's luck rests on its children.
source: Swedish folktale 'The Golden Cradle'

name: The Flower of Happiness
maker: Grows at Sunnymount Crest in the tale
powers: Possessing it was said to bring happiness.
description: The flower of happiness, the marvel of a tale told at Sunnymount Crest: a flower whose possession, or whose bloom, was said to bring happiness to whoever found it. In the tale the search for the flower tests the seeker, and the happiness it brings is measured in the finding rather than in any magic of the blossom itself. The tale belongs to the great European family of quests for a thing of pure good fortune, from the golden apple to the singing tree, where the journey works the change in the hero. At Sunnymount Crest the flower is tied to a real place, and the story shapes how the landscape is remembered. The flower is an object-lesson of the wonder-tale rather than a real plant, a reminder that happiness is found by those who seek it well.
source: Swedish folktale 'The Flower of Happiness'

name: The Cat of Norrhult
description: A bewitched cat in a folk tale from Norrhult in Småland. In the tale 'The Cat of Norrhult', a cat behaves in ways that betray a witch's or troll's power behind it, and the cat's strange actions reveal the magic at work in the village. Cats were the favourite disguise of witches and of the trolls' servants in Nordic belief, and a cat that walked on two legs, spoke, or wore something out of place was read as the true witch showing herself. The tale belongs to the wide Swedish family of stories about animals that are not what they seem, where the sharp eye of a neighbour or the luck of a household exposes the creature. In Norrhult the cat gives the village its name for the wonder, and the story still colours how the place remembers the event.
source: Småland folktale 'The Cat of Norrhult'

name: The Treasure in Säby Creek
description: A hidden treasure said to lie in a creek at Säby in Småland, at the centre of a Swedish folk tale. In the tale 'The Treasure in Säby Creek', the buried hoard is guarded or hard-won, and the treasure-seekers' venture into the creek tests their courage and luck. It belongs to the large Swedish family of tales about treasure guarded in the landscape, where gold lies under stones, in mounds, or at the bottom of waters, and where the guardian is a troll, a draug, or a burning light that marks the spot. Such tales taught that the treasure could be won only by the right person at the right hour, often on a holy night, and that greed or a misread sign cost the seekers everything. The creek at Säby keeps the promise and the warning of all such hoards.
source: Småland folktale 'The Treasure in Säby Creek'

name: The Sea King's Ring
maker: Given by the sea king in the ballad
powers: Binds the maiden to the sea king.
description: A golden ring given by the sea king in the Swedish ballad 'Agneta and the Sea King', a version of the old ballad about the maiden taken by the sea folk. The ring is the gift that binds the maiden to her underwater master, the token of a marriage that keeps her below the waves while her family mourns her above; in the ballad's ending the ring and its owner part in sorrow when the world above finally reclaims her. The ballad is documented in Swedish song collections from the 18th century and belongs to the international cycle of ballads about the seal-maiden and the water-man, in which a gift or a promise holds the human captive. The ring, like the sea king's crown, is the mark of the other world's power over the mortal who accepts it.
source: Swedish ballad 'Agneta and the Sea King'

name: The Madonna's Golden Shoe
maker: Belonging to the church Madonna statue
description: The golden shoe of the Virgin Mary's statue, at the centre of the Swedish tale 'The Fiddler Who Got the Madonna's Golden Shoe'. In the tale a fiddler who plays for the church is rewarded when the Madonna herself bestows her golden shoe on him, a gift from the living statue that proves his music found favour in heaven's eyes. The tale is one of Sweden's many stories of a church statue that comes alive, a motif with deep roots in medieval legend where painted Marys nod, weep, or reach out to the faithful. The golden shoe turns the church's most precious ornament into a personal blessing, and the fiddler's reward shows how music and devotion were judged the same act. The tale survives as a favourite of Swedish folk storytelling, told of several churches across the land.
source: Swedish folktale 'The Fiddler Who Got the Madonna's Golden Shoe'

name: The Broom King
maker: The broom itself in the tale
powers: Rules all brooms and sweeps away the story's dangers.
description: The broom king, the broom that rules all brooms, from the Swedish tale 'The Broom's Broom King of All Brooms'. In the tale a broom proves to be the king of its kind, sweeping away the story's dangers with a command that no other broom could match. The tale plays on the humble household object raised to kingship, a comic inversion in the spirit of the Scandinavian wonder-tales where the lowliest tool of the house shows the greatest power. The broom was in any case no ordinary thing in folk belief, being used to sweep out evil at the threshold, to sweep luck into the house at New Year, and as a mount in the lore of witches. Making the broom a king gathers all that magic into one homely hero, and the tale delights in seeing the farmyard champion reign.
source: Swedish folktale 'The Broom's Broom King of All Brooms'

name: The Cowbell of the Skogsrå
maker: Worn or carried by the forest spirit
powers: Its tinkling warns of the skogsrå's presence in the woods.
description: A cowbell heard in the forest in Swedish belief, and a mark of the skogsrå, the forest spirit who leads cattle astray. She is said to ring her bell or to ride a cow, and the tinkle of a bell where no cow is to be seen warns the woodsman or the herder of her presence. The cowbell ties the skogsrå to her trade of seducing cattle into the forest, where she keeps them in her care and returns them only on her own terms; a herd that wandered off was said to be 'with the skogsrå'. Her bell is a sound of both warning and temptation, for she appears as a beautiful woman from behind and a hollow or tailed thing when seen clearly. The cowbell is part of the skogsrå's folklore as a seductive and misleading spirit, whose call the wary were meant to resist.
source: Swedish belief about the skogsrå

name: The Luckstone
powers: Brings luck and wards off the mare and misfortune.
description: A luckstone (lyckosten), a stone with a natural hole, worn on a cord or kept in the pocket for luck and protection in Swedish folk tradition. Such pierced stones were also called 'hängesten', hanging stones, from the way they were strung and hung, and 'örngottsstenar'; they were hung in stables, on the neck, or by the bed to ward off the mare and misfortune, and the hole was the mark that gave the stone its power. In some districts the stone was hung over the stable door to keep the cattle safe, in others carried by sailors or travellers as a charm against storms and robbers. The lucky stone is known across the North Atlantic world as the 'witch stone' or 'hag stone', and the Swedish names record the same belief in the seeing and warding power of the pierced stone.
source: Swedish folk belief about pierced amulet stones

name: The Church Keys
material: Iron or brass key and a Bible
maker: Church key, used by the household
powers: Turns or shakes to reveal the name of a thief.
description: The church key used in the Swedish divination called nyckelprövning, the key test. A key was bound between the pages of a Bible, which was then hung or turned while names were read, and it was believed the key would point out or shake at the name of a thief. The key-and-Bible test is documented in Swedish folk tradition for finding stolen goods, and it was trusted because the church key and the holy book brought God's judgement into the search. The test belonged to the wider family of divination by the Bible, psalm, or sieve that country people used when the law could not find the guilty. Because the outcome could ruin a name, the practice was discouraged by the clergy, yet it lingered in villages into the 19th century as a feared and resorted-to last judgement.
source: Swedish folk tradition of the key-and-Bible test

name: The Black Book of the Clergy
powers: Conjurations and signs for summoning and binding spirits.
description: The black book (svartbok), a manual of black magic that Swedish tradition placed in the hands of a priest or 'klok' man who had studied 'the black art'. Actual svartkonstböcker, filled with conjurations, signs, and instructions, survive in Swedish archives from the 17th-19th centuries, and they mix prayers, biblical names, and runic-looking signs in the same hand that kept the parish register. Legend said the priest's black book could be passed on only on his deathbed, since the book had been given him by the powers of the dark and would burn or vanish if it fell to an unworthy hand. The book was used to find thieves, heal the bewitched, conjure answers, and bind spirits, and it made the clergy who owned it feared as much as respected. The black book stands at the meeting-point of church and folk magic, where the man of God was also the master of the dark art.
source: Swedish svartkonstbok tradition and archives

name: The Votive Ship
powers: A thank-offering that places the ship under the church's protection.
description: The votive ship (votivskepp), a model ship hung from the vault of a Swedish church, given in thanks for rescue at sea. Sailors and fishermen commissioned the models after storms, and hundreds still hang in Swedish churches and chapels, some with their rigging and little flags intact, carrying painted names and dates of the storm or the voyage. The ship joins the church's prayers to the sea's dangers, a documented custom from the late Middle Ages onward, and the models were made with such care that they are prized as records of old shipbuilding. The gift placed the ship, her crew, and their families under the protection of the church and its saints, and the model kept the vow alive as long as it hung. The votive ship is one of the most moving objects of Nordic church folk-culture, the sailor's thanksgiving made visible.
source: Swedish church votive-ship tradition
